moves.name: Defining the Central Problem
moves.signature: Articulating a general, unanswered question that motivates the inquiry.
moves.anchor: which polynomial equations are solvable by radicals?

moves.name: Bounding Prior Art
moves.signature: Identifying the limits of existing approaches to frame the need for a new method.
moves.anchor: had no general criterion

moves.name: Constructing a Formal Proxy
moves.signature: Associating a novel, structured object with each instance of the problem.
moves.anchor: associated to each polynomial a finite group of permutations of its roots

moves.name: Specifying Object Semantics
moves.signature: Defining the internal logic and constituent elements of the newly constructed object.
moves.anchor: defined as the automorphisms of the splitting field that fix the base field

moves.name: Forging a Property Equivalence
moves.signature: Demonstrating that a key property in the original domain maps directly to a specific property in the new representational domain.
moves.anchor: solvability by radicals corresponds exactly to the Galois group being a 'solvable group'

moves.name: Articulating a Decisive Criterion
moves.signature: Specifying the precise structural condition within the new domain that resolves the original question.
moves.anchor: a tower of normal subgroups with abelian quotients

moves.name: Translating the Core Inquiry
moves.signature: Reformulating the central problem entirely in terms of the properties of the new proxy object.
moves.anchor: the question 'is this equation solvable?' becomes 'does this group have a particular subgroup tower?'

moves.name: Migrating the Problem Space
moves.signature: Moving the locus of investigation from one formal discipline to another with more suitable tools.
moves.anchor: moves the problem from analysis to combinatorics of finite group structure

mappings.reason: Stating the motivating question is problem framing, not one of the listed theory-building operations.
Identifying limitations of existing methods is contextual framing rather than a structural operation in the vocabulary.
Associating a polynomial to a finite group creates a surrogate object through which the original solvability problem can be attacked.
Defining the proxy object's internal semantics is necessary formal setup but is not specifically captured by any listed operation.
It establishes that solving the surrogate group-theoretic property exactly resolves the original radical-solvability question.
The subgroup-tower criterion is the tractable surrogate-domain condition used to decide the original problem.
The original equation-solvability question is reformulated as a question about the associated group's structure.
The inquiry is shifted from equations to finite group structure as a more tractable surrogate domain.

moves.name: Engaging a Foundational Program
moves.signature: Addressing a central conjecture or challenge that defines the prevailing research paradigm in a field.
moves.anchor: Hilbert's program asked whether mathematics could be reduced

moves.name: Internalizing the Meta-Language
moves.signature: Devising a systematic scheme to represent statements about a system as statements within that same system.
moves.anchor: every formula in the formal system encoded as a natural number

moves.name: Translating Across Domains
moves.signature: Re-casting a problem from an external, descriptive domain into the native, operational domain of the system under study.
moves.anchor: statements ABOUT formulas became statements about numbers

moves.name: Establishing an Expressivity Condition
moves.signature: Identifying the minimum representational power a system must have for a specific self-analytic construction to be possible.
moves.anchor: the formal system was expressive enough to represent its own provability predicate

moves.name: Constructing a Self-Referential Object
moves.signature: Using a system's own rules to build an entity that makes a claim about its own status relative to those rules.
moves.anchor: construct a self-referential sentence

moves.name: Forcing a Paradoxical Choice
moves.signature: Creating a scenario where a system's own logic forces it into either contradiction or admitting its own limitations.
moves.anchor: 'this sentence is not provable in PA'

moves.name: Exposing an Inherent Limit
moves.signature: Demonstrating that any system of a certain type will necessarily have phenomena it cannot fully account for.
moves.anchor: any consistent formal system... is incomplete

moves.name: Barring Internal Self-Verification
moves.signature: Proving that a system cannot use its own internal mechanisms to formally establish its own soundness or reliability.
moves.anchor: cannot prove its own consistency

moves.name: Generalizing the Limitative Result
moves.signature: Abstracting a specific limitation into a universal principle applicable to all systems that meet a defined set of criteria.
moves.anchor: The same arithmetization technique generalized to other formal systems

mappings.reason: This is a choice of target problem within a paradigm, not a structural theory-building operation in the vocabulary.
It unifies meta-mathematical syntax with arithmetic by constructing a translation between statements about formulas and statements about numbers.
The move explicitly transfers problems from a descriptive meta-domain into the native arithmetic domain via a shared formal representation.
It identifies a threshold condition for self-representation, but does not itself import, lift, substitute, or force a solution in the vocabulary's sense.
Self-reference or diagonal construction is not directly represented by any listed operation.
The system's consistency constraints force a narrow dichotomy between contradiction and incompleteness.
A limitative impossibility result is not captured by the available constructive or translational operations.
The prohibition on internal consistency proof is a specific limitative result absent from the vocabulary.
Although it abstracts a theorem across systems, the vocabulary lacks an operation for generalizing impossibility principles.

moves.name: Formalize an Intuitive Notion
moves.signature: Define a vague, intuitive concept using a concrete, formal system.
moves.anchor: introduced the abstract machine — a finite-state controller reading and writing symbols on an infinite tape — as a formal model of mechanical computation.

moves.name: Assert Representational Completeness
moves.signature: Propose that the specific formal model is powerful enough to capture all relevant instances of the general concept.
moves.anchor: He defined 'computable' to mean 'computable by such a machine' (Church-Turing thesis).

moves.name: Construct a Universal Instance
moves.signature: Create an entity within the formal system that can simulate any other entity within that same system.
moves.anchor: He constructed a UNIVERSAL machine that, given as input the description of any other Turing machine plus that machine's input, simulates the other machine's computation.

moves.name: Pose a Self-Referential Problem
moves.signature: Formulate a problem where the system must analyze its own properties or the properties of its components.
moves.anchor: no Turing machine can decide whether arbitrary Turing machines halt.

moves.name: Import a Paradoxical Method
moves.signature: Employ a known logical technique that generates contradictions through self-reference to prove a negative claim.
moves.anchor: Using a diagonal argument structurally similar to Gödel's

moves.name: Establish an Inherent Limit
moves.signature: Demonstrate that a certain question cannot be answered by any procedure within the defined formal system.
moves.anchor: he showed the halting problem is undecidable

moves.name: Generalize the Negative Result
moves.signature: Show that the proven limitation within the formal model resolves a broader, pre-existing problem.
moves.anchor: This implied the Entscheidungsproblem has a negative answer.

moves.name: Leverage Universality for Limitation
moves.signature: Use a system's ability to represent itself to prove what that system cannot do.
moves.anchor: using the universality to construct undecidable problems.

mappings.reason: It turns the vague notion of mechanical computation into an explicit formal model.
The vocabulary lacks an operation for asserting that a formal model exhausts an intuitive concept.
A universal self-simulating interpreter within the same formal system is not captured by the listed operations.
Formulating a problem about the system's own components or behavior is absent from the vocabulary.
It adapts diagonal/self-reference methods from logic as an external proof technique.
Proving undecidability is a limit result rather than one of the listed theory-building operations.
It uses a formal reduction-like substitution to transfer the model-internal negative result to the broader Entscheidungsproblem.
Using universality and self-representation to derive impossibility is distinct from the available operations.
